arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Yang argued the enterprise need not have an ascertainable structure distinct from the predicate act.
Mr. Fernich argued the defendant has a right to an independent jury determination of each essential element.
Justice Ginsburg questioned the meaning of ascertainable structural hierarchy in the jury charge.

case.caption: Boyle v. United States

case_history.explanation: An official oral-argument transcript was verified.

case.dek: The dispute centers on whether a criminal group must have a distinct organizational structure beyond the specific crimes it commits to qualify as a RICO enterprise.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the definition of a RICO enterprise. the side that brought the case argues the law does not require a distinct structure. The government argues the group must be more than just the criminal acts themselves.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on January 14, 2009.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the conviction overturned because the jury did not find a distinct enterprise structure.
The government wants the conviction to stand because the criminal acts themselves formed the enterprise.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues RICO text and context show the enterprise definition is broad and lacks a structural limitation.
The government argues the jury must independently determine that the enterprise is more than a duplication of the pattern.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if the structure requirement applies only to the Brinks job.
Justice Ginsburg asked what the minimum requirement is to qualify as having a structure.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of federal racketeering laws. It determines whether prosecutors can charge individuals for criminal acts without proving a separate organizational hierarchy. The outcome shapes how courts interpret enterprise requirements in future RICO prosecutions.
